cases.title: Finca 470: an IDB road loan's forest offset and the Aché Kuetuvy's ten-year wait for title
cases.place: Finca 470, next to the Mbaracayú Forest Nature Reserve, Canindeyú department, Paraguay
cases.point: Mbaracayú Forest Nature Reserve (Wikipedia coordinates). Finca 470 is contiguous to the reserve; its own boundary was not found. Sources place it in different districts: the MICI panel says the district of Curuguaty, about 50 km from Curuguaty town; ABC Color says the district of Villa Ygatimí, about 60 km to its southeast.

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
lenders.role: Loan 933/OC-PR, Program to Improve Highway Corridors in Paraguay (PR-0035), approved by the Board in June 1996; loan contract signed 27 June 1996; first disbursement February 1998. The report gives two last-disbursement dates: 31 August 2009 in the Project Completion Report, and 30 December 2007, which Management told the panel on 1 May 2012 was the correct one. The report does not explain the gap. Bank policy at the time did not allow land to be bought with loan proceeds, so Clause 4.05 of the loan's special conditions committed Paraguay to buy the offset land with its own counterpart funds: up to US$4 million for conservation areas and US$2 million for indigenous communities.

cases.conditions: The loan's Environmental Sub-Program required Paraguay to buy 20,000 hectares for forest reserves and 11,000 hectares to regularise indigenous land ownership, as an offset for the social and ecological impacts of future road works. The December 1995 Environmental Summary had set out ten conditions to be met before loan approval and before first disbursement, including a land-titling plan naming the indigenous communities to benefit, the hectares and funding for each, and a timetable for acquisition and demarcation. The MICI panel found this phased approach was never written into the loan contract and never put into effect.
cases.community: Finca 470 is about 4,600 hectares (Management; the panel elsewhere says approximately 4,760). The Moisés Bertoni Foundation was finalising a purchase of it from its Taiwanese owner, who also owned a nearby sawmill, in order to title it to the Aché. Those talks collapsed when the Ministry of Public Works and Communications bought the land at a higher price to meet the loan's offset requirement. MOPC handed it to the environment ministry SEAM in 2003; SEAM ceded temporary usufruct to the indigenous institute INDI in 2004 so the Aché Kuetuvy could continue their way of life, with a process to follow for legal transfer. The Aché developed and ran a certified forest management plan, funded by Conservation International, and met IDB staff in Asunción repeatedly between 2001 and 2007; IDB funds paid a Paraguayan lawyer to advance the titling. They still had no title ten years later. On 21 June 2010 a new SEAM administration issued Resolution 662 authorising transfer of Finca 470 to the Aché Kuetuvy and also to the Avá Guaraní of Ytu and Tekoha Ka'a Poty. The Avá Guaraní living on the edge of the finca are campesinos in extreme poverty who need land for small-scale farming; the Aché told the panel they would give several hundred hectares to the five Avá Guaraní families long resident there but opposed an influx from further away. Global Voices reports that on 26 July 2012 the government transferred about 4,600 hectares to the Aché of Kuetuvy, after sixty families had fought nine years for it.
cases.suppression: The chair of the MICI compliance review panel wrote on 20 November 2012 that reports from Paraguay indicated a group of heavily armed illegal loggers had invaded Finca 470 from May 2012 onwards, threatening violence against the Aché and cutting down large trees sold as illegal timber. Global Voices, citing ABC Color, reports that peasant groups issued death threats to Aché who tried to stop the logging and to journalists covering it, and that on 15 August 2012 at 19:30 the community leader Margarita Mbywangi took a call from a man identifying himself as a peasant who said that if young Aché hunters came near them they would be killed. The people making these threats were invaders and loggers, not the lender or a project contractor.
cases.killed_note: The Requesters told MICI that in the spring of 1992 the Aché were expelled from the area that now includes Finca 470 and forcibly moved to a reservation 100 km to the south-west, and that an estimated 40 per cent of the community died as a result, which led to international allegations of genocide. This was before the IDB loan and is not counted here. Reported by the Requesters in the panel report, not a panel finding.
cases.ecosystem: The panel wrote that the environmental component of the project must be judged to have failed: the hectare targets were not reached and, aside from a few exceptions, notably Finca 470, much of the forest land that should have been protected in perpetuity had been unsustainably logged or completely cleared. The panel also recorded being alerted to the deforestation of a 1,600-hectare area that MOPC had bought for conservation. Management's own account says the 1,600 hectares were still under negotiation and about to be bought; no source explains that gap. A panel annex says land bought by Paraguay to meet the IDB offset targets had already been largely deforested, and suggests giving it to the Avá Guaraní because it would suit their farming. Canindeyú had lost an estimated 87 per cent of its forest ecosystem by the 1990s. The 64,405-hectare Mbaracayú reserve and Finca 470 next to it were the parts still largely intact, described to the panel as an island of trees in a sea of agro-business expansion. The Interior Atlantic Forest has been reduced to less than 5 per cent of its original range.
cases.outcome: The panel found the IDB failed to enforce compliance with the Environment Policy (OP-703), Project Preparation, Evaluation and Approval (OP-302) and Operations Administration (OP-304), and that this failure was an important cause of the harm the Aché alleged. It said the project interfered in an almost completed purchase of Finca 470 on behalf of the Aché, and that the later shortage of properly managed social offset land led SEAM to propose giving a large part of the promised land to an Avá Guaraní group that had not helped manage it. Portfolio reviews in 2004 and 2005 found the consolidated land-purchase plan only partly implemented and the loan clauses on land for protected areas and indigenous peoples in full or partial non-compliance. The government transferred title to the Aché Kuetuvy on 26 July 2012, after the panel's draft report had circulated.

cases.confidence_note: IDB Management told the panel that loan 933/OC-PR financed no upgrading or paving work on Route 10, only work on Route 3, so the Aché sit in the indirect area of influence of a road the Bank never financed; on that basis Management called the harm argument irrelevant and outside MICI's remit, and said the Aché had usufruct, which it considered a legally viable way of meeting the project's objective. The panel found non-compliance anyway and said the Aché claim of harm was valid, because the offset purchase the loan required is what blocked the transfer of title to them. The panel's own wording about harm to the community is forward-looking: breaking the promise of title 'threatens to bring direct material harm to them as a community and as individuals'. What the panel records as having already happened is the blocked purchase, the ten years without title, and the logging or clearing of offset land. The 1992 expulsion and death toll are the Requesters' account, not a finding. The death threats of 2012 come from Global Voices citing ABC Color.
cx: Program to Improve Highway Corridors in Paraguay

lvwhy.land: The loan required Paraguay to buy 20,000 ha of forest reserve and 11,000 ha for indigenous communities as an offset; the purchase of Finca 470 under that requirement is what blocked the sale that would have titled the land to the Aché.
lvwhy.project: The money was a road programme loan, and the offset land purchases were a condition of it.

cases.whole: Management says Paraguay spent US$4,411,794 on 8,365 hectares of uncultivated land, including 1,600 hectares still under negotiation, and US$2,375,000 on 10,975 hectares for indigenous communities, of which 1,000 hectares were bought with local funds through INDI and 4,600 hectares were Finca 470, first bought as an environmental protection area. Elsewhere in the same response Management says two lots totalling 6,765 hectares were bought for woodland conservation and that about 9,375 hectares went to seven indigenous communities. The committed targets were 20,000 and 11,000 hectares. Management explains the shortfall by delays pushing up land prices between design in 1993-96 and the last disbursement; the panel says the offset strategy lacked realism about land availability and counterpart funds from the start. Separately, the panel records that The Nature Conservancy and the Moisés Bertoni Foundation bought the adjacent Mbaracayú Forest from the International Finance Corporation for US$2 million in 1991, after the IFC took the land as collateral when a Paraguayan timber company defaulted on an IFC loan, with USAID, the energy company AES and other donors contributing; a condition of that sale was that the Aché's claims to continued use be respected.

cases.title: Medupi power station: sand mining damage to the Mokolo River and graves on the plant site
cases.place: Medupi Power Station and Marapong, Lephalale, Limpopo, South Africa
cases.point: Medupi Power Station (Global Energy Monitor coordinates)

lenders.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
lenders.role: Loan for the Medupi Power Project to Eskom Holdings Ltd; Board voting date 25 November 2009. Early Warning System, drawing on AfDB data, records AfDB funding of 1,689,982,912 units of account and does not disclose a US dollar figure. The IRM's fifth monitoring report of 28 January 2022 says the project is fully disbursed and the Bank no longer supervises implementation.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: US$3.75 billion Eskom Investment Support Project loan, described in the Inspection Panel's investigation overview as the largest World Bank loan to date, with Eskom as borrower and the South African government as guarantor. The Panel received the request for inspection on 6 April 2010 and the Board discussed its investigation report on 22 May 2012.

lenders.name: Other lenders named by Global Energy Monitor
lenders.role: China Development Bank US$1.5 billion (July 2017); New Development Bank US$480 million (April 2019) for sulphur dioxide abatement; KfW US$353.31 million; and US$721.98 million from BHF Bank, BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole, Commerzbank, KfW, Natixis and UniCredit. These figures are Global Energy Monitor's; no independent check was found.

cases.conditions: The AfDB loan agreement required Eskom to obtain water permits from the Department of Water Affairs for expanded access to the Mokolo Dam (Phase 1) and an integrated permit for the planned Phase 2 of the Mokolo-Crocodile Water Augmentation Project, and to develop boreholes. The IRM found the only reference to water in the loan document was that permit requirement, that it lacked enough specificity to ensure compliance with Bank policy, and that the condition had not been fulfilled as at December 2011.

companies.name: Eskom Holdings SOC Ltd
companies.role: Borrower, developer and operator of the 4,800 MW station; carried out the sand mining in the Mokolo River through its contractors and dealt with the graves on the site
companies.desc: South Africa's state-owned electricity utility, registration number 2002/015527/30, named by Early Warning System as the borrower for the AfDB loan and by the World Bank Inspection Panel as the borrower for the US$3.75 billion IBRD loan.

cases.community: Marapong, next to the older Matimba station and a few kilometres from Medupi, had a population of about 17,000 at the time of the IRM review. The requesters, two South African nationals who asked to stay anonymous, filed with the IRM on 28 September 2010. They said communities near the plant were subjected to removals and to the desecration of ancestral graves, and would bear hidden health costs from air pollution, sulphur dioxide and mercury in their water, air and land, constrained water access and degradation of land and water in a largely agrarian area. On graves, the IRM found no sufficient assessment had been done to determine whether graves existed and that consultation was insufficient, and that the Bank failed to establish the gravesites and the significance attached to them. Management said there were only two graves on the site: an old one, for which an affidavit was produced and which Eskom relocated to a formal cemetery, and the grave of a child whose mother had agreed in principle to relocation but was being prevented from signing. The IRM's fifth monitoring report records that Eskom then ran a heritage assessment, identified graves on the Medupi site, held cleansing and appeasement ceremonies with the affected families and built a memorial site, and that further steps were needed to secure the families' access to it; a protocol of regular engagement was later agreed. The IRM compliance report says there was one relocation: an occupant of one of the farms was moved, with his consent, by the farm owner to another of his farms.
cases.killed_note: No deaths attributed to the project in the documents read. Global Energy Monitor cites a Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimate of about 90 pollution-related deaths a year if the plant runs without flue gas desulphurisation; that is a modelled projection, not a count of deaths, and is not counted here.
cases.ecosystem: The IRM's monitoring reports record that sand mining in the Mokolo River, carried out to supply construction material, was suspended after what the IRM called unnecessary delays, and that the community was waiting for an answer about rehabilitation of the damaged areas of the river. The IRM concluded that the environmental assessment done for a sand mining licence application could not substitute for an independent assessment of the damage done to the Mokolo River and of the rehabilitation needed after earlier legal and illegal sand mining. The Department of Mineral Resources investigated, closed the matter, and concluded that Eskom could not be responsible for rehabilitating all the mined areas. Eskom's own annual emissions report for April 2025 to March 2026 records 12 exceedances of the 3,500 mg/Nm3 monthly average sulphur dioxide limit on its atmospheric emission licence, all at Unit 4 in February 2026 and all attributed to a faulty continuous emissions monitoring system; 40 exceedances of the 50 mg/Nm3 daily particulate matter limit, of which 22 were within the start-up and shutdown grace, 12 were attributed to faulty monitoring and 6 were reported as section 30 incidents; and 12 readings above the 750 mg/Nm3 nitrogen oxide limit, also attributed to faulty monitoring. The same report says the area around Medupi's ambient monitoring site is non-compliant with the national ozone standard, which Eskom attributes to multiple sources including third parties, and that there were no exceedances of the daily PM10, daily SO2 or hourly NO2 ambient limits in 2025. Two of 20 dust fall-out buckets exceeded the 1,200 mg/m2/day non-residential limit: point D15a six times, peaking at 4,645 mg/m2/day in October 2025, and point D5a three times, peaking at 3,979 mg/m2/day in October 2025. The IRM and the Inspection Panel both treated ash-dump leaching and operational-phase air and water degradation as risks rather than as damage already done.
cases.outcome: The IRM's compliance review, dated 19 December 2011 and led by Daniel Bradlow and Richard Bissell, found the Bank out of compliance on water: it failed to explain in the project appraisal report how it complied with the Integrated Water Resource Management Policy, and the loan documentation lacked the specificity needed. On land and water degradation the IRM found it could not reach a firm conclusion about compliance before Medupi became operational. On sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and mercury it found the Bank complied with the applicable policies at the analysis stage. A Management Action Plan set nine commitments, including a graves and heritage assessment process, follow-up on sand mining, groundwater monitoring and a grievance centre. The Accountability Console records all nine as incomplete. The fifth monitoring report of 28 January 2022 says the IRM suspended annual monitoring until at least 2026, because construction is complete, the Bank no longer supervises implementation and the project is fully disbursed, and that the two pending action items are expected to be implemented within five years.

cases.confidence_note: What is recorded as having happened is damage to the Mokolo River from sand mining for the construction, graves on the plant site that required a heritage assessment, cleansing ceremonies and a memorial, one grave relocated to a formal cemetery, one farm occupant relocated with his consent, and measured exceedances in Eskom's own emissions reporting. Attribution of the river damage is partly disputed: the Department of Mineral Resources concluded that Eskom could not be responsible for rehabilitating all the mined areas, and the IRM said no independent assessment of the damage from earlier legal and illegal mining had been done. The health harm the requesters alleged is not established. The IRM wrote that the people of Marapong are understandably nervous that sulphur dioxide is causing ill health among a population already in poor health, and that the lack of good public data on respiratory illness rates makes that worse; it did not find that the emissions had caused illness. Management's cited assessment put the potential for infrequent mild respiratory effects in Marapong at moderate, with the threshold exceeded four times a year. The Inspection Panel likewise described risks rather than confirmed harm, noting many impacts would only materialise once the plant was operating.

lvwhy.project: The money built a 4,800 MW coal station; the sand mining and the graves both sit on or beside the construction works.
lvwhy.finance: The AfDB loan's only water clause was a permit requirement, which the IRM found unfulfilled and too vague to secure compliance.

cases.whole: The station has six units of 800 MW, 4,800 MW in all. Global Energy Monitor dates commercial operation unit by unit: unit 6 synchronised to the grid in March 2015, unit 5 on 3 April 2017, unit 4 on 28 November 2017, unit 3 on 28 June 2019, unit 2 in November 2019, and unit 1 synchronised in August 2019 with the last unit in commercial operation in late July 2021. Flue gas desulphurisation was designed in but, as the Inspection Panel noted, full installation was planned only three years after full operation, and wet FGD sharply increases water demand. The IRM found that as of December 2011 the Department of Water Affairs had not decided whether to proceed with the Mokolo-Crocodile Water Augmentation Project that the scrubbers depend on.

cases.title: Polihali Dam, Lesotho Highlands Phase II: cracked houses, relocations and falling land rates
cases.place: Polihali Dam and the villages of Masakong, Ha Tlhakola, Tsekong and Lits'otsong, Mokhotlong district, Lesotho
cases.point: Polihali Dam on the Senqu River (Wikipedia coordinates). The affected villages lie around the dam and along the access roads and transfer tunnel, in Mokhotlong and Leribe districts.

lenders.name: African Development Bank (AfDB)
lenders.role: Approved a US$86.72 million loan to co-finance Phase II, reported by Engineering News on 11 October 2021. The funds are used by South Africa's Trans-Caledon Tunnel Authority and the Lesotho Highlands Development Authority implements the part inside Lesotho. The loan covers the Polihali dam and reservoir, a 38 km transfer tunnel, roads and bridges, telecommunications and the extension of electricity and other infrastructure in Lesotho. Engineering News puts the total project cost at US$2.17 billion.

lenders.name: New Development Bank (NDB)
lenders.role: Co-financier. Engineering News reported on 21 August 2023 that the NDB would provide a R3.2 billion loan to the Trans-Caledon Tunnel Authority for Phase II. Accountability Counsel lists the NDB alongside the AfDB, the Development Bank of Southern Africa and the TCTA as co-financiers.

lenders.name: Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA)
lenders.role: Co-financier. Engineering News reported on 4 June 2021 that the TCTA and the DBSA closed a R5.5 billion deal for Phase II.

cases.conditions: Not extracted. The AfDB publishes a resettlement action plan summary for the project; its terms were not read for this entry.

companies.name: Lesotho Highlands Development Authority (LHDA)
companies.role: Implementing authority inside Lesotho; runs the compensation and resettlement programme and is the respondent in the Lesotho High Court case and the AfDB complaint
companies.desc: The Lesotho body that implements the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, established under the LHDA Order of 1986. Its spokesperson is Mpho Brown.

companies.name: Trans-Caledon Tunnel Authority (TCTA)
companies.role: South African state-owned authority that uses the AfDB, NDB and DBSA loans for Phase II
companies.desc: A South African state-owned entity that raises finance for and manages bulk water transfer infrastructure, named by Engineering News as the borrower and user of the AfDB, NDB and DBSA Phase II loans.

cases.community: About 1,600 villagers from 18 rural mountain communities filed a complaint with the AfDB's Independent Review Mechanism, dated 11 September 2025 and since registered, supported by the Seinoli Legal Centre and Accountability Counsel. The LHDA's own account, given to Mining Weekly in April 2025 through its statement and the resettlement manager Mpaleng Oliphant, is that 270 households have been identified for relocation, that about 11,700 assets are affected, that 21 business structures are to be relocated and that more than 570 graves have been relocated with more scheduled at reservoir-affected sites. By then 9 households in Liphofung had been relocated in 2023 because of the transfer tunnel quarry in Leribe, and 4 households in Lits'otsong had been moved to Makalong in Mokhotlong in 2024. Nine replacement houses had been built since January 2022 for households affected by the Polihali access roads, at Checheng, Mapholaneng, Makokoaneng, Ha Sekila, Phakoeng and Ha Poli. New resettlement sites at Tloha re Bue and Ha Ramonakalali are to take households from Tloha re Bue, Masakong and Ha Tlhakola, with at least 64 houses planned. Public Eye reports the Ombudsman's finding that families in unfinished resettlement houses were left without promised water, electricity and access roads. Complainants also say grazing land has been fenced, access to forest for firewood and medicinal plants lost, traditional paths blocked by access roads, rocks thrown onto fields by excavation and harvests reduced, that women are excluded from compensation and decision-making, and that an influx of male workers has raised safety and health concerns. In a separate constitutional case in the Lesotho High Court, the Mokhotlong Business Forum Development Trust, representing more than 489 registered companies, and the Community Resources Development Trust, with more than 3,000 individuals, say land was expropriated for over 37 years without fair compensation, that cattle are dying for lack of pasture, and that a promised community development fund was never set up.
cases.suppression: Complainants allege harassment or arrest when they protest, including placards confiscated at a sod-turning in May 2023 and a police assault at Ha-Seshote and Liseleng. The High Court applicants allege that community members who resisted were arrested, detained, tortured and prosecuted by police working with LHDA agents. Seinoli alleges some people were made to sign agreements under threat of expropriation without compensation. These are the complainants' allegations; no finding on them was found.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the documents read.
cases.displaced_note: LHDA figures via Mining Weekly, April 2025: 9 households at Liphofung in 2023 and 4 at Lits'otsong in 2024, out of 270 households identified for relocation. Nine replacement houses were built from January 2022 for households affected by the Polihali access roads, but the article does not say how many of those households had moved in. The Ombudsman has ordered three further villages relocated within six months.
cases.ecosystem: Wikipedia says the dam is 165 m high with a total capacity of 2,325 million cubic metres, and that the dam and the filling of the reservoir will affect more than 5,000 hectares of land. Complainants say blasting raises heavy dust with a strong chemical smell and contaminates nearby water sources, so that women walk long distances for water when sources are polluted or pipes are damaged, and that grazing land has been fenced and forest access lost. The Ombudsman rejected the LHDA's position that some villagers found the dust manageable and called for sound barriers and regular watering.
cases.outcome: In June 2026 the Lesotho Ombudsman, Advocate Tlotliso Polaki, issued a report after investigating. Public Eye reports that the Ombudsman's investigators found houses with severe structural cracks and at least one complete house collapse in Masakong and Ha Tlhakola, attributed to blasting and heavy machinery, and judged the pace of repair dangerously slow. The LHDA submitted data on 19 March saying 48 damaged houses had been repaired, 24 under the dam project and 20 under the tunnel project; Public Eye notes that those two figures add to 44, not 48, and no source explains the gap. The Ombudsman ordered the LHDA to relocate the three villages within six months, pay direct redress to affected households, finish unfinished houses with the promised services, and give interim livelihood and financial support. On compensation, Public Eye reports Phase I arrears of M142.2 million as at 31 December 2025 with future costs projected at M473 million, and Phase II arrears of M6.76 million with future costs near M25 million, and that the rate paid for expropriated land fell from M23 per square metre to as little as M0.98 in some areas and M0.68 in others, with no clear explanation from the LHDA. GroundUp reports the rate in Kanana-Mabothong and Popa falling from R23 per square metre in 2023 to 98 cents in 2024. The AfDB's IRM registered the complaint; as of 17 February 2026 Accountability Counsel said AfDB Management had not said clearly whether it would join mediation, and that blasting continues and relocation remains incomplete. Seinoli and Accountability Counsel wrote to the New Development Bank's president and board on 19 June 2026 saying engagement since August 2024 had produced no meaningful response.

cases.confidence_note: The house damage is the Lesotho Ombudsman's own finding, reported by Public Eye: severe structural cracks and at least one complete collapse in Masakong and Ha Tlhakola, attributed to blasting and heavy machinery. The relocations, the 11,700 affected assets and the more than 570 relocated graves are the LHDA's own figures, given to Mining Weekly. The LHDA denies the broader allegations: its spokesperson Mpho Brown told GroundUp that consultations are ongoing, compensation is fair, over R154 million has been paid for private assets with 93 per cent of acquired assets compensated, and that no homes have been declared uninhabitable. The dust, water contamination, intimidation and gender claims rest on the complainants' accounts and are reported here as such. This is Phase II at Polihali in Mokhotlong, a different dam and different communities from the Phase 1 case at Katse already on the map.
cx: Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II (Polihali Dam)

lvwhy.land: Land was expropriated for the reservoir, the access roads and the transfer tunnel, and the rate paid per square metre fell sharply between 2023 and 2024.
lvwhy.project: The loans finance the dam, the 38 km tunnel and the access roads whose blasting and construction the harm follows.

cases.whole: Engineering News puts the total Phase II cost at US$2.17 billion; Wikipedia gives the dam's cost as M7.68 billion. Construction of the dam began in August 2023, with opening planned for 2028. The scheme is to raise Lesotho's hydropower capacity and increase water exports to South Africa's Vaal River system. The High Court applicants say Phase II construction began in March 2015 but the approved scheme was only published later that year. A Sixty15 joint venture resettlement housing contract worth R372.8 million was awarded in October 2024.

dropped.candidate: MICI-PE-2015-0094 Rural Land Titling PTRT-3, Peruvian Amazon
dropped.reason: Fails test 2. I downloaded and read the full English public final MICI Compliance Review Report for PTRT-3 (PE-L1026, loan 3370/OC-PE), document id EZIDB0000559-1009163277-2745 from mici.iadb.org, 4,349 lines of extracted text. I read the whole determination section II.E (paragraphs 2.141 to 2.163) and conclusions 3.1 to 3.4 line by line, and searched the entire text for every occurrence of 'harm', 'deforest', 'displac' and related words. MICI found non-compliance with OP-703 directives B.3, B.4, B.5, B.7 and B.9 and with OP-765, and the Accountability Console records the compliance review as closed with non-compliance found on 16 April 2025. Every harm statement is hedged. Paragraph 2.148 is headed 'Potential harm' and says the lack of meaningful consultation 'may have made it impossible' to ensure participation. Paragraph 2.152 says misclassification 'may have left undetected risks and adverse impacts'. Paragraph 2.163 says the gaps 'could have exacerbated the vulnerability' of lands, environment, health and culture. On deforestation, paragraph 2.160 says the environmental assessment identified deforestation as the main problem in the jungle and recognised it 'could be a consequence' of titling, and MICI's only finding is that it could not find evidence the Bank monitored the prevention programme. The one thing recorded as having happened, in paragraph 2.156, is that failure to meet titling targets 'gave rise to frustration, disillusionment, and a sense of having been cheated' and that communities 'still lacked legal security of tenure' - a failure to deliver a benefit, not land, income, health or life lost. I also read the MICI monitoring report (EZIDB0000559-1009163277-2959, 1,416 lines) and found no record of harm having occurred; its one use of the word is to describe the original allegations. The brief forbids un-hedging a likelihood, so this is a drop.
